To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there are encouraging trends towards increased capacity of CD4 and HIV viral load (HVL) instruments in reporting countries, but the capacity of available HVL instruments is inadequate in many countries, and the capacity of available instruments is not being utilized in most countries.
there is a global shortage of HIV testing technologies, especially for viral load and early infant diagnosis testing, and that these shortages are most pronounced in low- and medium-income countries.
the global capacity to test for HIV and CD4 count is adequate, but the capacity to test for viral load is not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the availability and use of technologies used to monitor the HIV epidemic and the treatment of HIV-infected individuals in WHO Member States.
the availability and use of HIV technologies in WHO Member States from 2012–2013.
the availability of HIV technologies and the use of these technologies in 127 countries, and the data were obtained through a WHO survey conducted from 2011 to 2013.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the availability of HIV testing technologies is improving but the utilization and performance of these technologies are inadequate in most countries.
, while the availability of CD4 and EID technologies in WHO Member States is encouraging, their utilization is inadequate.
there are significant gaps between the availability and use of CD4 and viral load testing in many countries.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the survey results suggest that there is a need for major operational changes to be implemented in low- and mid income countries, if the targets are to be achieved.
the availability of CD4 and viral load testing is increasing in many countries, but utilization remains low.
there is a need to improve laboratory infrastructure and to increase the capacity for CD4 and VL testing in order to meet the ambitious 90-90 targets.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to improve the capacity to monitor HIV treatment outcomes and the use of available technologies to ensure that the HIV epidemic can be brought under control.
the HIV treatment monitoring and EID infrastructure needs to be expanded and strengthened to ensure that all people who need to be tested are tested, and those in need of treatment are treated.
there is a need for more accurate and timely reporting of laboratory technology utilization, particularly in low-income settings.
